questions.q: What exercise does the book recommend for finding your WHY?
a: Recounting 10 to 12 past events that had a big impact on you
Listing the skills you could sell to the highest bidder
Asking colleagues to rate your strongest personality traits
Writing a five-year plan with measurable career targets
questions.why: Lesson 1 says old stories, told to someone who asks good questions, reveal your purpose.

questions.q: What are your HOWs in this framework?
a: The attitudes and behaviors that let you do your best work
The goals you must reach before your purpose can count
The people who will fund your first business venture
The reasons your previous jobs failed to satisfy you
questions.why: Lesson 2 defines HOWs as the habits and viewpoints that shape how you work.

questions.q: How does the summary suggest identifying your HOWs?
a: By reviewing past routines and the skills you have built
By copying the working style of someone you admire
By taking a standardized personality test online
By asking your manager to define them for you
questions.why: Lesson 2 says past behavior is the best guide to how you should work.

questions.q: What is one benefit of telling people your WHY often?
a: It keeps forcing you to sharpen how you state it
It guarantees investors will support your next idea
It stops other people from questioning your choices
It lets you avoid explaining what you actually do
questions.why: Lesson 3 lists constant refinement of your mission statement among the reasons to share it.

questions.q: What did the steel company owner's example show about purpose?
a: The product matters less than the larger impact behind it
Only exciting industries can give people a sense of mission
Businesses must choose between profit and meaningful work
Old industries are usually the easiest to feel passionate about
questions.why: Lesson 1 says his WHY was a cleaner environment, not the steel itself.
